subject:
WATCH: Walmart found a creative, illegal way to make sure they have
 the lowest prices.
body:
They're forcing companies to raise prices on any competitor who dares to sell items at a lower price than Walmart.

Hi Joshua willems, it’s Faiz from More Perfect Union.

The conventional wisdom is that Walmart's prices are lower because of scale and efficiency. On the other hand economists say Walmart is able to keep prices low because of advertising revenue.

The truth: They're forcing companies to raise prices on any competitor who dares to sell items at a lower price than Walmart.

That’s right, instead of lowering prices to offer the lowest price, Walmart is forcing their competitors to charge you more. It’s not competition. It’s corporate greed.

Watch our exclusive report and then sign and send a message to your members of Congress calling for the passage of the Fair Competition for Small Business Act now.

CONTACT CONGRESS

Independent grocers are vital to communities nationwide, acting as a crucial source of employment, food access, and economic stability in both urban and rural areas. Data from the National Grocers Association shows that these independent businesses support over 1.1 million jobs and contribute more than $41 billion in annual wages.

Walmart uses their market power to secure discounts and favorable payment terms from suppliers that smaller grocers lack the leverage to negotiate. As a result, independent grocers get charged higher prices for the same products -- which is why congress passed the Robinson-Patman Act to make that tactic illegal.

Here’s the deal: Walmart gets around it because federal regulators don’t enforce the law, leaving small businesses to fend for themselves.

The Fair Competition for Small Business Act authorizes state attorneys general to bring civil actions for damages against distributors and retailers that engage in unlawful price discrimination under the Robinson-Patman Act.

This new legislation closes the gap between the law and enforcement by giving your attorney general the same enforcement authority states already have under other federal antitrust laws.

That’s how we fix it, but first watch our report exposing the truth and how we caught Walmart’s clever, but illegal way to make sure they offer the lowest prices by clicking here.

In solidarity,

-Faiz

Faiz Shakir, Co-Founder
More Perfect Union

What's Changing?

Developers and creators share one ecosystem but have different objectives, challenges, and paths to success. We’ve decided to evolve our ecosystem into two distinct platforms, each with its own focused strategy, and each designed for long-term sustainability.

Here's a quick look.

VR

- We’ll continue to focus on helping third-party apps and games succeed to unlock more opportunities for developers.
- We’re updating the Meta Horizon Store so developer games and apps take center stage instead of Worlds.
- Better discovery and monetization tools are on the way to help you generate revenue and grow your business on Quest.

Worlds

- Mobile-first worlds are now the default so creators can reach a wider audience.
- We’re designing dedicated tools to help you build mobile worlds that look better, load faster, and retain people for longer.

We’re going all-in on the people building with us, and we can’t wait to see where you take it. Get the full details below.

subject: Facility Update – Drainage and Ongoing Improvements
body:
Dear Joshua Willems,
I hope this message finds you well.
My name is Andy DR, Owner and Manager of Secure Storage Units in Oakdale, CA. I am writing to inform you that due to the recent heavy rainfall across the Central Valley, our facility’s drainage system has been temporarily overwhelmed. As a result, there is some standing water in certain drive areas and near a few unit doors.
We have already contacted a highly recommended local contractor, referred by the City of Oakdale, who will be onsite this afternoon to assess the situation and implement a corrective plan as quickly as possible. Please be assured that we are treating this matter with urgency.
I would also like to thank the customer who promptly brought this to my attention — I truly appreciate the communication and partnership in maintaining the quality of the facility.
Additionally, since acquiring the property several years ago, we have been steadily investing in upgrades to improve security and overall condition. This includes the installation of new and additional security cameras, as well as the phased replacement of older roll-up doors.
If your unit has an older door and would like a new one installed and/or you experience any issues with your roll-up door, PLEASE do not hesitate to contact us by calling our main office line or emailing me directly at SecureStorageUnits@gmail.com. I am committed to ensuring your unit remains secure and fully functional.
Thank you for your continued trust in Secure Storage Units.
Sincerely,
Andy DROwner & ManagerSecure Storage UnitsOakdale, CA

subject: Love, but make it tidal 💙🌊🐟

https://click.email.montereybayaquarium.org/?%3D%3D 




Aquarium updates




Full hearts and hopeful horizons



 With gratitude for an extraordinary legacy and excitement for what’s ahead, we’re proud to share an important leadership transition for the Aquarium. After a global search, we are thrilled to welcome Dr. Jenny Gray as the Aquarium’s Chief Executive Officer—a position endowed through the generosity of longtime donor Nancy Burgermeister. One of the most influential zoo leaders in the world and a passionate champion for conservation, Jenny brings decades of experience advancing wildlife protection, research, and animal well-being. Originally from South Africa she is widely respected for her bold, forward-thinking leadership in the global conservation community.

Her appointment represents a new wave of opportunity for the Aquarium. As we honor the legacy that has guided us here, we look ahead with gratitude, momentum, and a shared commitment to protecting our blue planet.


https://click.email.montereybayaquarium.org/?%3D%3D 
Read more about Dr. Gray in her interview with the LA Times 




Plenty of fish in the sea



They say there are plenty of fish in the sea—but have you ever stopped to think about what those fish are actually doing down there? Beneath the waves lies a world of unexpected romance, intricate partnerships, and perfectly-timed seasonal rendezvous that would put any dating app algorithm to shame. From clownfish couples who mate for life to coral reefs that synchronize their spawning with the moon, the ocean is basically one giant lesson in connection, cooperation, and cosmic timing. Welcome to ocean hopecore: where biodiversity meets belonging, where every creature finds its niche, and where love—in all its weird, wonderful forms—flows with the tides. Dive in with us as we explore what the sea can teach us about relationships, resilience, and the beautiful truth that
 we're all just looking for our school to swim with.


https://click.email.montereybayaquarium.org/?%3D%3D 
Explore different ocean habitats 






Love is in the… water?



As hefty winter swells rumble along the Central Coast, marine animals get down to the serious business of passing on their genes. Large predatory fish like lingcod and cabezon lay sticky egg masses, which the dutiful dads guard for weeks until they hatch. Meanwhile, the water itself gets a little… hazy, as other animals release their reproductive cells straight into the water column. Many invertebrates (that’s animals without a backbone) such as abalone, mussels, sea stars, and sand dollars are broadcast spawners and rely on perfect timing rather than romance. When conditions are right, they shoot eggs and sperm into the water. Once one animal starts the spawning party, everyone else joins in, dramatically boosting the odds of successful fertilization. So cue up the Marvin
 Gaye, set out the chocolate-dipped strawberries, and dive in. Monterey’s underwater love-fest is in full swing!


https://click.email.montereybayaquarium.org/?%3D%3D 
See how we grow sand dollars from egg to exhibit 





(c) MBARI


 Spongey, shrimpy, deep-sea romantasy



On the deep seafloor, glass sponges like the Venus’ flower basket filter food through delicate silica lattices, drawing shrimp into their shimmering halls. This mutualistic bond turns the sponge into a living keep—shrimp tend to glassy halls, grazing away excess food, while the Venus’ flower basket rewards them with protection, shelter, and a bountiful feast. Scientists have observed some shrimp mates swear lifelong allegiance within these crystal walls—mating, raising young, and eventually growing too large to leave their throne of glass. A deep-sea love story more fantastical than fiction!


https://click.email.montereybayaquarium.org/?%3D%3D 
Meet more fantastical sponges on MBARI’s website 






A symbiotic love



It’s a relationship built on protection, survival, and mutual benefit: clownfish often find sanctuaries in the tentacles of anemones, while anemones receive a nutrient boost from their finned tenants. The clownfish chases off predators, and its special mucus keeps it safe from stings—a true “mucus-match" made in the reef. These species aren’t codependent, yet they can thrive together, reminding us that sometimes the strongest bonds are built on trust, teamwork, and a little splash of hope. 


https://click.email.montereybayaquarium.org/?%3D%3D 
Discover more about the clownfish 




 Don't miss






https://click.email.montereybayaquarium.org/?%3D%3D 




Love takes flight in every language

Tufted puffins are gearing up for the breeding season in early spring with bright orange beaks and devoted hearts. They reunite each spring, reinforcing pair bonds that can last for years. When it’s time to breed, the tufted puffin returns to its birth colony—often reuniting with the same mate. Talk about true love. Our newest bilingual video celebrates this season of love and dives into the fascinating life of tufted puffins! 


https://click.email.montereybayaquarium.org/?%3D%3D 
Learn more about the tufted puffins in Spanish 




Wallpaper
Appreciating the extraordinary in the seemingly ordinary. City pigeons might surprise you, they actually have coastal roots. Pigeons descend from rock doves that once nested along sea cliffs, which is why ledges, bridges, and buildings feel like home. They’re incredible navigators, capable of finding their way across long distances, and many form long-term pair bonds and share parenting duties. On top of all that, these clever birds can recognize human faces, see more colors than we do, and they can recognize themselves in puddles and mirrors. Tough, loyal, and quietly adaptable, pigeons remind us that love and resilience often show up in the most familiar places, even right outside our window.

https://click.email.montereybayaquarium.org/?%3D%3D 
Download the wallpaper 




Help us continue our urgent conservation work
From addressing climate change to ending plastic pollution, restoring ecosystems and improving seafood sustainability—together we can help protect the ocean for future generations.
https://click.email.montereybayaquarium.org/?%3D%3D 
Donate now

subject: When You Cross a Sovereign Border
body:
View this post on the web at https://anonymous8675309.substack.com/p/when-you-cross-a-sovereign-border

There is a line that exists in the world that is more than dirt, wire, paint, or water. It is not merely geographic. It is legal. It is moral. It is civilizational.
A sovereign border is the physical expression of a people choosing to exist together under a shared agreement. That agreement is a nation. Not just land. Not just government. A nation is a contract between the living, the dead who built it, and the unborn who will inherit it.
When someone crosses a sovereign border they are not simply stepping into a new location. They are entering a covenant.
Citizens are born into that covenant and bound by it. Immigrants may enter it by invitation. Visitors are permitted to temporarily exist under its protection. But in every case the same principle applies: the laws of that nation are now the authority over you while you stand within it.
Borders therefore are not about exclusion. They are about definition.
Without borders there is no legal jurisdiction. Without jurisdiction there is no law. Without law there is no protection. And without protection there is no nation, only territory waiting to be claimed by whoever is strongest at the moment.
Every country on earth recognizes this truth whether they admit it publicly or not. The first duty of any government is not welfare, not diplomacy, not economy. The first duty is preservation of sovereignty. Because every other function collapses if the authority of the border collapses.
When a person crosses illegally they are not just bypassing paperwork. They are rejecting the legal authority that gives them the protections they seek. They are asking to receive the benefits of a covenant while denying the legitimacy of the covenant itself.
Law cannot operate selectively. A nation cannot be half sovereign. Either its borders define its authority or they do not. And if they do not, the nation exists only in memory.
Citizenship is therefore not simply residence. It is allegiance.
Allegiance means accepting the laws even when inconvenient, the responsibilities even when costly, and the identity even when unpopular. It is a pledge that the nation’s survival matters more than individual preference because without the nation, individual rights cannot exist.
A person may come from anywhere on earth and become part of a people. History proves this repeatedly. But they must enter the covenant honestly. Not by force, not by manipulation, not by erasing the boundary that defines it.
Because once a border no longer matters, the people within it no longer have a say in their own future. Their laws become suggestions. Their votes become symbolic. Their nation becomes an address rather than a society.
A sovereign border is therefore sacred in the civic sense. It is the point where chaos ends and ordered liberty begins.
And ordered liberty requires loyalty.
Not to politicians. Not to parties. To the nation itself and the principles that give it existence.
When you cross a sovereign border you are stepping under a flag that represents the authority of a people to govern themselves. To accept its protection while rejecting its legitimacy is not neutrality. It is opposition.
Because a nation cannot survive if those within it refuse the bond that holds it together. If you do not like the laws of this sovereign nation, if you are complicit of crimes against the republic and have participated in these acts, you should start making travel arrangements. 
If you do not pledge allegiance, it is treason.

subject: [PODCAST #628] 👉  Thinking & Feeling Misreads: Stop Second-Guessing Your Type
body:
If you are second guessing your type it might be the way the functions are described.
 
 

Hi Joshua,

 

If you’ve ever read a personality type description and thought, “Well… I can do that,” or “That can’t be me... those people sound awful,” you’re not alone.

 

In our newest episode, we unpack why you might keep circling the wrong type, even when you’ve been studying this for years.

 

The problem is that many online descriptions highlight a type's best traits or its worst stereotypes. People read it and try to match that to their lived experience. Add in burnout, culture, and identity bias... and suddenly your “type journey” turns into a loop of second-guessing.

 

👉 Listen now and step beneath the surface and recognize what’s really driving the confusion, so you can stop chasing labels and start spotting patterns.
Watch or Listen To The Podcast ⮕
 

Can We Get Your Advice?
Antonia and I are shaping the podcast for the coming season and we’d love your input & advice. We created a quick 2-minute check-in to learn what you actually need right now. Your guidance will help us build the most relevant tools and topics over the next few weeks.

👉 Share Your Advice » (2 min)
 

Most people aren’t “bad at typing themselves.” They’re reacting to biased descriptions, behavior stereotypes, and the very human urge to claim what sounds smart, and avoid what sounds harsh.

 

This week, you’ll learn:

  • Why some cognitive functions get “glowing” write-ups… while others get the “wet firecracker” treatment (and how that skews your self-assessment).

  • How behavior-based stereotypes cause mistypes, and what it means to return to a function’s “nucleus.”

The most common misreads of the judging functions:

  • Harmony: burnout can make FJ types think they’re introverts, and culture can mask it.

  • Accuracy: “I’m smart and I research” isn’t the same as Introverted Thinking’s obsession with clean thinking processes.

  • Effectiveness: it’s not “being mean,” it’s results + resource management (and most mature TJs are softies inside).

  • Authenticity: over-identifying with everything can keep you stuck. Clarity comes from what you want and what you can’t stop doing.

If you’ve ever thought, “I could be any type,” or “none of the descriptions fit,” this episode will help you sort signal from noise.

 

Listen now and get a clearer read on what’s actually happening in your thinking & feeling.

 

👉 Which function do you think you’ve been misreading, and how has it affected your type journey?

 

<— Hit reply and share your experience with us.

 

We released this podcast in both video and audio this week.
Watch or Listen To The Podcast ⮕
 


Much Love,

Joel Mark Witt & Antonia Dodge
Co-Founders | Personality Hacker

How filing early pays off              Expecting a refund? Filing
early means you’ll get your funds sooner. Usually owe money?
You’ll have more time to pay. And with a head start, you’ll get
the chance to carefully review every last tax break, not hurry
past potential dollars back.       All your tax forms should be
available now, so there’s nothing standing in your way. Tap to
reveal why these forms may be needed and where to find them.
Common tax forms and what they're for/where to find them. Form
W-2 for wages and taxes withheld from an employer; Form 1099-INT
for interest earned from banks or credit unions; and Form

subject: God Is Not Fooled by Your Routine
body:
View this post on the web at https://anonymous8675309.substack.com/p/god-is-not-fooled-by-your-routine

There is a comfort in routine. We wake at the same hour, repeat the same prayers, sit in the same seat, speak the same words, and call it faithfulness. Outwardly it looks disciplined. It looks devoted. It even looks holy.
But God is not impressed by repetition that replaces relationship.
Human beings measure devotion by consistency. God measures devotion by sincerity. We count attendance, memorization, and visible effort. He searches motives, intentions, and the quiet places of the heart that no one else sees. A person can perform every religious action and still be completely absent where it matters most.
Routine can become a disguise.
We learn what to say. We learn when to stand, when to kneel, when to bow our heads, and when to raise our hands. Over time the body participates while the heart withdraws. Lips move but the mind wanders. Words are spoken but never felt. We fulfill the habit and assume heaven receives it.
Yet God does not listen to sound alone. He listens to truth.
He is not fooled by the prayer spoken while resentment is guarded, by the worship sung while pride is protected, or by the confession offered without repentance. The outward act may be correct while the inward reality remains untouched. Ritual without surrender becomes performance, and performance cannot transform a soul.
The danger is subtle because routine feels safe. It allows us to believe we are growing while we are only repeating. It creates the illusion of progress without the cost of change. We can do religious things for years and never actually encounter God because we learned how to approach Him mechanically instead of honestly.
God does not want a schedule. He wants you.
He is not seeking perfect wording but genuine need. Not impressive prayers but truthful ones. Not long speeches but surrendered hearts. A single honest cry reaches Him faster than a thousand practiced phrases spoken without meaning.
Faith was never designed to be a script. It was meant to be a living relationship. Relationships breathe, struggle, question, confess, and sometimes sit in silence. They are not powered by memorization but by connection.
Many people fear breaking routine because routine feels like obedience. Yet obedience is not repetition. Obedience is alignment. It is the willingness to let God interrupt your patterns, confront your attitudes, and change your direction. Real faith allows God to correct you, not just comfort you.
You cannot hide behind spiritual habits. God sees the bitterness you justify, the forgiveness you delay, the humility you avoid, and the truth you resist. He is patient, but He is not deceived.
The purpose of prayer is not to complete it. The purpose is to mean it.
So pause before the next familiar words leave your mouth. Ask yourself whether you are speaking to God or reciting at Him. Silence may be more faithful than empty repetition. A broken sentence may be holier than a polished speech.
God is not fooled by your routine, but He is moved by your sincerity.
He is waiting not for perfection, but for honesty.

NEW FEATURE: New Preview Interface 🎞️

Hi Joshua,

 

You now get a larger, faster video preview built directly into the editor, along with a visual timeline that shows scene thumbnails. Jump to any scene in one click, move to the exact second you want, and see your edits update in real time so you can fine-tune pacing, flow, and structure before you generate and download.

This update gives you more control and saves you time when editing videos in Pictory.

Edit a video with the New Preview → ( https://app.pictory.ai )

Play ( https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UVCIsXXISBc )

Here's what you can do with the New Preview Interface..
*******************************************************

* View your video playback in a larger preview panel.

Use the interactive timeline to jump to any scene by clicking its thumbnail.

We built this update so you spend less time guessing and more time creating. Try it out now in the Pictory editor! ( https://app.pictory.ai )

If you need any help, reply to this email and I'll get back to you asap!

Happy Creating!

Hi Joshua,

Thank you for reaching out about posting a review.

To assist you, could you please first confirm the name of the caregiver youd like to post a review for?

If youre having trouble submitting the review, please try the following troubleshooting steps:

Use a different browser (for example, Chrome, Firefox, or Safari).
Clear your browsers cache and cookies, then close and reopen the browser.
Try using a different device (such as a mobile phone, tablet, or another computer).
Make sure your browser is updated to the latest version.

If the issue continues, please send us a screenshot of what you see when you try to post the review, including any error messages or unusual screens. This will help us better understand and resolve the problem.

Once we have the caregivers name and more details about the issue, well be happy to look into this further for you





If you have any further questions or concerns, please visit our Help page.

Best Wishes,
Yara

subject: [Care Ministry: Prayer Sheet] TLC Prayer Sheet 2/17
body:
TLC Prayer Sheet 2/17

The other other day, I was driving Baby D and arrived at a
three way intersection. -The one by the Rispin Mansion and the
Capitola Library in case you were wondering. And of course I
stopped like a good driver and looked all directions. But then I
got momentarily distracted thinking I saw someone I knew walking
in the new Rispin Mansion park, and then proceeded to start my
right turn. But in the moments I had been looking away, there was
now a couple walking in the intersection, and so I braked and
waved my apology. It w was of course my error, but I was going
very slow and stopped after just barely starting to turn. And I
was expecting a little wave in return at my apology wave.

But I did not get that. I didn't even get the middle finger.

The girl never even bothered a glance, so either she had complete
faith in the pedestrian walkway, or complete faith in the boy she
was with. Or perhaps she was welcoming a slight tap from a car in
the crosswalk in hopes of a juicy juicy settlement.

But the male in question, looked at me with utter disdain and
disbelief. Then he continued to stare at me and gave me a hang
loose sign, a peace sign, and then laughed and shook his head the
whole rest of the way across. As if I was the dumbest idiot in
the whole wide world and he would never make such a foolish
foolish mistake. And hey, perhaps he hasn't -maybe he is
Pedestrian Peter and with the patience and graciousness of a
Saint, he makes sure every granny, child, and duckling makes it
all the way across the road every single time. Or perhaps he's
just kinda a jerk.

Can you imagine what it would be like that's what happened when
we went to the Lord? If we mustered up the courage, the will, the
humble posture of our heart, and said "Lord, I was wrong, I have
sinned. Please forgive me," and in return he just scoffed at us.

The great news is, that is very much Not what the Lord does.

Which is great, because next time I see that rude boy while I'm
driving, I just might knock him over. And then of course, I'll
have to ask the Lord for forgiveness, so it's wonderful that He
will be so gracious! (This is of course a joke-not the Lord's
graciousness, my bad actions)

But it is wonderful that we serve a Heavenly Father who is
gracious and kind and forgiving.

Isaiah 43:25 (NIV): "I, even I, am he who blots out your
transgressions, for my own sake, and remembers your sins no
more."

Psalm 86:5 (NIV): "You, Lord, are forgiving and good, abounding
in love to all who call to you."

Micah 7:18-19 (NIV): "...You will again have compassion on us;
you will tread our sins underfoot and hurl all our iniquities
into the depths of the sea."

And the other good news is, while my human nature might scream at
my perceived injustices (how dare they not accept my driving
apology and then in turn try to make me feel like a dum dum!) the
Holy Spirit in me whispers the reminder to forgive others, just
as Christ has forgiven me. And while this is good news because it
will save me from acting out of anger and doing something
actually stupid, (Baby D you wait in the car, Mama is gonna go
kick some annoying boy's booty!), it also really is good news
because how much lighter and freer are we when we forgive. -A
lot.

And if you're like me, and you have a slightly...or more than
slightly, vengeful nature, the best advice I ever heard on
forgiving, was to keep doing it. Not just for different people or
different situations, but sometimes the same person and the same
situation requires a continual heart of forgiveness.

And the other good news is, there will never (on earth) be an end
of situations or people that cause us to work on our forgiving
spirit, so you will have plenty of opportunities to practice!
Goody haha.

subject: Stephen Colbert’s YouTube exclusive
body:
Joshua willems,

Democratic State Rep. James Talarico, who is running for Texas’s Senate seat this year, was all set to appear on The Late Show with Stephen Colbert last night, until a phone call came in from CBS ordering Colbert not to air the interview.

CBS cited a memo from Trump’s FCC chairman, Brendan Carr, threatening to revoke ‘equal time’ exemptions for interviews with political candidates. Even though Carr’s memo was just a threat, not policy, CBS wanted to comply in advance.

Why would CBS do this? For the same reason that they announced that Colbert’s show would end at the end of this season: To curry favor with the Trump administration ahead of planned mergers. Last summer, CBS parent company Paramount was in the midst of a merger with David Ellison’s Skydance, and now the Ellisons are trying to take over Warner Bros.

All of these mergers require government approval -- and the Trump administration has made it clear that it will leverage that approval to make powerful corporations bend the knee.

Watch the interview that CBS didn’t want you to see, then sign our message thanking Stephen Colbert for standing up to power!

Thank You Stephen!

Colbert made it incredibly clear what was happening:

Donald Trump’s administration wants to silence anyone who says anything bad about Trump on TV because all Trump does is watch TV.

We founded More Perfect Union to be working-class media that addressed working-class problems. What Brendan Carr and the Trump administration are trying to do is turn all broadcast media into outlets for corporate propaganda.

It’s critical for people with platforms in broadcast media like Stephen Colbert to stand up to this administration’s attempts to silence dissent and trample the First Amendment.

When people stand up, the way Stephen Colbert did, they need to know the public supports them. Signing a thank you card may seem silly, but it sends a message not just to Colbert, but to the next person that Trump tries to silence too.

Add your voice! Watch Colbert’s interview, then sign a thank you card!

In solidarity,

-Faiz

Faiz Shakir, Co-Founder
More Perfect Union

SUPPORT OUR WORK

subject: "Power" Walking
body:
View this post on the web at https://robwalker.substack.com/p/power-walking

Hey y’all. Happy Lunar New Year, and Happy Mardi Gras (and if you get to this a little later then Happy Ash Wednesday and Happy Ramadan).
Today: walking. As if it weren’t a virtuous enough and constantly recommended activity already, The New York Times now suggests (gift link [ https://substack.com/redirect/cfca2384-f7c1-42d0-84dd-aa7ee1815293?j=eyJ1IjoiMm15YTc5In0.a5QmJPQwfPYQ8VH1roFp4vKV6p4E_sWIcjzGfYjlMgQ ]) it can be a first step toward civic reform. 
Specifically, The Times and Citizen University propose a form of walk that amounts to “an exercise for mapping civic power in a geographic space.” 
Look around your neighborhood, Citizen University suggests [ https://substack.com/redirect/8870e03a-6251-4be8-9f05-f2d84bd11386?j=eyJ1IjoiMm15YTc5In0.a5QmJPQwfPYQ8VH1roFp4vKV6p4E_sWIcjzGfYjlMgQ ]: “Have you ever wondered… how did things come to be this way? Who made the choices that shaped this place? And what’s changing right now, often without us noticing?”
The Times writes: 
At its core, the Power Walk is a new lens through which to see a neighborhood, guided by a series of prompts to reflect on what could change and where capacity exists to change it. It’s a way of understanding the possibilities that people see in the world around them, and discussing what collective power they have to realize those possibilities.
The Times article [ https://substack.com/redirect/cfca2384-f7c1-42d0-84dd-aa7ee1815293?j=eyJ1IjoiMm15YTc5In0.a5QmJPQwfPYQ8VH1roFp4vKV6p4E_sWIcjzGfYjlMgQ ] tells the story of citizens reshaping a lower Manhattan neighborhood, including the conversion of unused land into a public park. It all started with locals looking around and asking questions about what could change, and how.  
To help encourage such outcomes elsewhere, Citizen University has made a Power Walk field guide [ https://substack.com/redirect/8870e03a-6251-4be8-9f05-f2d84bd11386?j=eyJ1IjoiMm15YTc5In0.a5QmJPQwfPYQ8VH1roFp4vKV6p4E_sWIcjzGfYjlMgQ ], and I really like some of the questions
These questions prompt you to attend to and consider your neighborhood in new ways, even if you don’t have specific ideas for changes.  And who knows — after a walk or two, maybe you’ll have a few!
(That Times article, by the way, ends with a call-out to anyone interested in trying a Power Walk wherever you are. Go here [ https://substack.com/redirect/cfca2384-f7c1-42d0-84dd-aa7ee1815293?j=eyJ1IjoiMm15YTc5In0.a5QmJPQwfPYQ8VH1roFp4vKV6p4E_sWIcjzGfYjlMgQ ] and scroll to the form at the bottom if that might be you!) 
Noticing is about other people, too. The Icebreaker series aims to help with that. There’s a central collection spot for all the icebreakers to date, here [ https://substack.com/redirect/7bf5bc4a-ebad-4f84-b0a8-19c45c02e2e4?j=eyJ1IjoiMm15YTc5In0.a5QmJPQwfPYQ8VH1roFp4vKV6p4E_sWIcjzGfYjlMgQ ].
Today’s Icebreaker comes from Melvin Adekanye:
“What three words would your friends use to describe you?”
Melvin is a bona-fide icebreaker expert! He’s the founder of JamSocial [ https://substack.com/redirect/65251f44-c210-4d48-a619-e32bf9bfbe74?j=eyJ1IjoiMm15YTc5In0.a5QmJPQwfPYQ8VH1roFp4vKV6p4E_sWIcjzGfYjlMgQ ], a platform for starting conversations and connections at events. More about their Jam Bingo game here [ https://substack.com/redirect/9bfd2bca-77ee-4554-bc14-1d57f846f6a8?j=eyJ1IjoiMm15YTc5In0.a5QmJPQwfPYQ8VH1roFp4vKV6p4E_sWIcjzGfYjlMgQ ]. 
To me this question inspires two spinoffs — what three words do you wish they would use, and (hardest to answer in conversation, I suppose) what three might you fear?
Thank you so much, Melvin!
Please send your favorite icebreaker (whether you made it up or found it elsewhere) to consumed@robwalker.net [ mailto:consumed@robwalker.net ].
SUPPORT TAoN
If you enjoy TAoN, please become a paid supporter [ https://substack.com/redirect/157cee1b-ccc0-4a23-91ce-e66efa8cdb60?j=eyJ1IjoiMm15YTc5In0.a5QmJPQwfPYQ8VH1roFp4vKV6p4E_sWIcjzGfYjlMgQ ]. You’ll get access to the full archives as well as supporter-only bonus posts and discussion threads. Your support makes this newsletter possible. 
—> ALSO: Check out the recent TAoN creative-attention Zoom workshop [ https://substack.com/redirect/2be27073-97db-4da1-8382-ab574da18a4c?j=eyJ1IjoiMm15YTc5In0.a5QmJPQwfPYQ8VH1roFp4vKV6p4E_sWIcjzGfYjlMgQ ] on turning moments into haiku, led by writer/photographer/traveler Lisa Germany [ https://substack.com/redirect/7242cb4c-2ae8-495f-a9aa-bfd6302e0189?j=eyJ1IjoiMm15YTc5In0.a5QmJPQwfPYQ8VH1roFp4vKV6p4E_sWIcjzGfYjlMgQ ].
Thank you!
IN OTHER NEWS
Spurious Correlations (example above). I love this project [ https://substack.com/redirect/37ca0d24-4afa-4c32-936c-ea4d53cb3fb5?j=eyJ1IjoiMm15YTc5In0.a5QmJPQwfPYQ8VH1roFp4vKV6p4E_sWIcjzGfYjlMgQ ] so much. (Via Kottke [ https://substack.com/redirect/bca82ca7-137e-4d56-b91b-506d8492d322?j=eyJ1IjoiMm15YTc5In0.a5QmJPQwfPYQ8VH1roFp4vKV6p4E_sWIcjzGfYjlMgQ ])
Badass Olympic skeleton-racer helmets [ https://substack.com/redirect/aa9ca91a-b0e0-4133-8e34-b7818ffd7837?j=eyJ1IjoiMm15YTc5In0.a5QmJPQwfPYQ8VH1roFp4vKV6p4E_sWIcjzGfYjlMgQ ].
“Rather than keeping a diary, I started keeping notebooks. Where a diary constructs narrative, character and voice, a notebook is inherently fragmented, allowing for unexpected glimmers of serendipitous juxtaposition and lyric voltage.” Essay [ https://substack.com/redirect/3bbd8d5b-4b23-4f72-83ff-a8e152d95cd3?j=eyJ1IjoiMm15YTc5In0.a5QmJPQwfPYQ8VH1roFp4vKV6p4E_sWIcjzGfYjlMgQ ] By Daniel Poppick
An online museum [ https://substack.com/redirect/6dfb37c0-54d6-4249-bc3f-e21354e64917?j=eyJ1IjoiMm15YTc5In0.a5QmJPQwfPYQ8VH1roFp4vKV6p4E_sWIcjzGfYjlMgQ ] of Typographic Objects. (Via Heller, who has an interview [ https://substack.com/redirect/57819aea-dd60-47ad-b40c-de76490f2d7b?j=eyJ1IjoiMm15YTc5In0.a5QmJPQwfPYQ8VH1roFp4vKV6p4E_sWIcjzGfYjlMgQ ].) 
Book cover designer Oliver Munday on [ https://substack.com/redirect/b78842ba-4cd8-45aa-9275-33be93a122a4?j=eyJ1IjoiMm15YTc5In0.a5QmJPQwfPYQ8VH1roFp4vKV6p4E_sWIcjzGfYjlMgQ ] someone else designing his book’s cover. 
“The earliest known example of possible operative dental work dates to approximately 14,000 years ago in northern Italy.” Fun fact from this piece [ https://substack.com/redirect/0a9819f1-c6ed-48b7-95c8-c9bc14f0661a?j=eyJ1IjoiMm15YTc5In0.a5QmJPQwfPYQ8VH1roFp4vKV6p4E_sWIcjzGfYjlMgQ ] about why earlier humans had straight teeth without braces. 
Street art [ https://substack.com/redirect/bae6dcfb-e861-4bac-96e6-9ad41f5ae88b?j=eyJ1IjoiMm15YTc5In0.a5QmJPQwfPYQ8VH1roFp4vKV6p4E_sWIcjzGfYjlMgQ ] interacting with reality. 
“This page intentionally left blank.” Why that is [ https://substack.com/redirect/445ef0a0-2ea0-4c16-bea4-567a8ca33020?j=eyJ1IjoiMm15YTc5In0.a5QmJPQwfPYQ8VH1roFp4vKV6p4E_sWIcjzGfYjlMgQ ]. 
KBB on [ https://substack.com/redirect/66949926-f081-45d7-99df-d3324304be25?j=eyJ1IjoiMm15YTc5In0.a5QmJPQwfPYQ8VH1roFp4vKV6p4E_sWIcjzGfYjlMgQ ] 20 years of drawing stuff she bought, and “the strange comfort of repetition.”
OKAY THAT’S IT!
As always, I value your feedback (suggestions, critiques, positive reinforcement, constructive insults directed at me, not at anyone else, etc.), as well as your tips or stories or personal noticing rituals, things we need a word for, and of course your icebreakers [ https://substack.com/redirect/a06e4862-0fc0-4747-93f8-ab4d75a42cd1?j=eyJ1IjoiMm15YTc5In0.a5QmJPQwfPYQ8VH1roFp4vKV6p4E_sWIcjzGfYjlMgQ ]: consumed@robwalker.net. Or use the comments.
—> Or just click the heart symbol. That always makes my day.
And thanks for reading …

subject: The Ring of Fire Eclipse
body:
View this post on the web at https://anonymous8675309.substack.com/p/the-ring-of-fire-eclipse

There are moments in history when humanity looks up together.
No borders
No politics
No noise
Just the sky
And on those rare days the heavens appear to write in light
The Ring of Fire eclipse is one of those moments
When the Sun Became a Halo
An annular solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes directly between Earth and the Sun but is slightly farther away in its orbit. Because of that distance it cannot fully cover the Sun’s disk. Instead it leaves a blazing circle of light around the lunar silhouette, a perfect ring.
A crown
A halo
A fiery seal suspended in the firmament
Scientists at NASA describe it as a predictable orbital alignment governed by mathematics and celestial mechanics. And they are correct.
Yet mathematics does not remove meaning
It never has
For thousands of years civilizations interpreted eclipses as messages. Not because people were ignorant but because they understood something modern culture often forgets
When the entire sky changes it matters
The Path Across the Earth
During the great Ring of Fire alignment the shadow carved a narrow path across the world touching ancient lands and modern cities alike
It crossed parts of Mexico
Then swept across Texas
And brushed portions of Florida in partial shadow
Millions stopped what they were doing
Workers paused
Children pointed
Drivers pulled to the roadside
Even skeptics stared
Because when daylight turns unnatural something inside human beings awakens, a primal awareness older than language
For a few minutes time felt different
The Silence During Alignment
Birds quieted
Wind seemed to hesitate
Temperature dipped
Not dramatically and not catastrophically but noticeably
Nature responds to light more than we realize. When the Sun’s presence is altered the Earth reacts as if evening suddenly arrives in the middle of day
Many described the experience the same way
It felt sacred
Not religious necessarily but reverent
You could feel the scale of existence
You could feel how small we are and how connected
Ancient Fear and Modern Awe
In the ancient world eclipses often brought fear because they broke expectation. The sky was dependable and the Sun rose every day. Order ruled the cosmos
Then suddenly darkness at noon
Kings consulted priests
Armies halted battles
Entire cultures recorded eclipses as turning points in history
Today we know orbital mechanics and can predict eclipses centuries in advance
Yet something fascinating happens
Even knowing the science people still feel wonder
Because explanation removes mystery but not significance
The equations tell us how
They never fully answer why it moves us
The Symbolism of the Ring
A circle has always represented completion covenant and continuity
A wedding ring
A crown
A seal
The Ring of Fire eclipse uniquely combines light and shadow, not destruction of the Sun but framing it
Darkness cannot consume the light
It outlines it
And that image resonates deeply with human psychology and spiritual intuition alike. Across cultures the ring represents protection and promise
The eclipse becomes a cosmic illustration
The light remains even when hidden
A Shared Sky in a Divided Age
Perhaps the most remarkable part of any eclipse is not astronomical but social
For a brief moment millions experience the same event simultaneously
No algorithm decides what you see
No broadcast filters it
No institution interprets it first
You witness it directly
The sky belongs to everyone
In a world increasingly mediated by screens and narratives an eclipse reminds humanity of unfiltered reality. You cannot scroll past it and you cannot debate it into nonexistence
You simply stand beneath it together
What People Felt
After the eclipse passed reactions were strangely consistent across different backgrounds
Calm
Perspective
Gratitude
Reflection
Some felt spiritual peace
Others felt scientific curiosity
Many felt both
Because events of this scale touch both hemispheres of the human mind, logic and meaning
Eclipses endure in memory long after they occur not because they are rare but because they restore a sense of place within creation
The Message of the Moment
The Ring of Fire eclipse did not change governments
It did not stop wars
It did not rewrite economies
But it did something subtler
It interrupted human certainty
It reminded us that above our daily conflicts a vast clockwork continues, precise and immense, indifferent to division
Yet at the same time it invited unity
Everyone who looked up saw the same circle of light
For a few minutes humanity shared a single experience older than civilization itself
After the Light Returned
Daylight came back quickly
Conversations resumed
Traffic moved again
Phones buzzed
But people walked away different
Not transformed permanently yet touched by perspective
The Ring of Fire eclipse leaves behind a quiet question
If the sky can still bring the world to silence for a moment what else might we rediscover if we occasionally looked up instead of across
We live beneath the same Sun
We move within the same design
And certain parts of the world will see it today

subject: 143. A Photograph Is Not a Telephone
body:
View this post on the web at https://markmcguire.substack.com/p/143-a-photograph-is-not-a-telephone

As the story goes, on March 10, 1876, Alexander Graham Bell, working in his lab in Boston, accidentally spilled acid on himself and called out to his assistant through his experimental device: “Mr Watson, come here — I want to see you.” Watson, in another room, heard the words clearly and came to his aid. That sentence is generally regarded as the first successful voice transmission by telephone.*
We sometimes think that photography is like telephony — that a picture is a message sent from the photographer to the viewer. With some genres of photography, notably documentary and photojournalism, explanatory text and captions often support a particular story and point of view that the photographer, author, and publisher work together to communicate. However, if the link between image and text is broken and the image floats free, it can attach itself to other narratives or prompt the creation of new ones.
A photographer who prefers to let a photograph speak for itself might find that what he or she believes the photograph is saying is not what the viewer is hearing. When I see a photograph that someone has exhibited, published in a book, or shared online, and I read what they have to say about it, I am often struck by how their reading differs from mine.
A photograph isn’t a news report that tells you the facts; it’s more like a poem that triggers memories and associations. It doesn’t carry a story — it invites you to create your own. What it lacks in authority, it makes up for in potential. The provenance of an image can matter less than the authenticity of the story it helps you create.
The only text that can honestly accompany a photograph is a question mark or an ellipsis that asks: What do you think? What do you make of this?
A photographer can tell the story of how a photograph came to be, but like a child who has left home, no one can predict what it will do in the world. It carries traces of its origins, but it will have a life of its own.
__________
*Alexander Graham Bell, notebook entry, 10 March 1876, Alexander Graham Bell Family Papers, Library of Congress, https://www.loc.gov/loc/lcib/9903/edison.html [ https://substack.com/redirect/7257ff04-67fa-49be-a3bb-114f5744e047?j=eyJ1IjoiMm15YTc5In0.a5QmJPQwfPYQ8VH1roFp4vKV6p4E_sWIcjzGfYjlMgQ ]
Spotlight
This week, I’d like to shine a light on Artificial Intelligence and recommend a Substack post and a podcast. 
Minimum Standards for Taking AI Seriously [ https://substack.com/redirect/f0bc2edb-b878-48b9-9335-391f2035b08a?j=eyJ1IjoiMm15YTc5In0.a5QmJPQwfPYQ8VH1roFp4vKV6p4E_sWIcjzGfYjlMgQ ] from How Things Work [ https://substack.com/redirect/c34d35ed-296a-4a67-a6cd-ae39ef1376ba?j=eyJ1IjoiMm15YTc5In0.a5QmJPQwfPYQ8VH1roFp4vKV6p4E_sWIcjzGfYjlMgQ ] by Hamilton Nolan  
Anyone involved in photography, writing, or other creative pursuits should be following efforts to replace creative human labour with bots in the pursuit of increased productivity and profits.  
This is a thoughtful Substack post by Hamilton Nolan about Artificial Intelligence, with useful links. The focus of his Substack is on “power, how it is wielded, and how it can be channeled for the common good.”
I’m a regular listener of the New York Times Hard Fork [ https://substack.com/redirect/67fc8e2a-4040-4514-9dfc-60efdcc7ccd0?j=eyJ1IjoiMm15YTc5In0.a5QmJPQwfPYQ8VH1roFp4vKV6p4E_sWIcjzGfYjlMgQ ] podcast [ https://substack.com/redirect/67fc8e2a-4040-4514-9dfc-60efdcc7ccd0?j=eyJ1IjoiMm15YTc5In0.a5QmJPQwfPYQ8VH1roFp4vKV6p4E_sWIcjzGfYjlMgQ ], which covers technology — especially Artificial Intelligence. The banter between the hosts is witty and entertaining, and the information is both helpful and up to date. You can read the piece they mention by Matt Schumer, Something Big Is Happening [ https://substack.com/redirect/0f8e7483-14eb-4643-94d5-708fd4af8135?j=eyJ1IjoiMm15YTc5In0.a5QmJPQwfPYQ8VH1roFp4vKV6p4E_sWIcjzGfYjlMgQ ] (Feb. 9, 2026), about how fast AI is advancing and what it could mean for the future of employment, here [ https://substack.com/redirect/0f8e7483-14eb-4643-94d5-708fd4af8135?j=eyJ1IjoiMm15YTc5In0.a5QmJPQwfPYQ8VH1roFp4vKV6p4E_sWIcjzGfYjlMgQ ]. 
I recently read a story in my local newspaper about an AI startup that helps to “create insights from every conversation” by generating meeting minutes, SWOT analyses, decision logs, action items, risk registers, board meeting minutes, jobs-to-be-done frameworks, user stories, key themes, struggles, needs, empathy maps, LinkedIn articles, case studies, news stories, PR releases, social media posts, and cheatsheets.
I think there’s a market for an AI assistant that attends lectures, takes notes, writes summaries, sits exams, applies for jobs, exceeds every expectation, wins Employee of the Year on day one, gets promoted, takes over the company, fires the staff, puts the operation on automatic (co)pilot, and then spends the rest of its days in the lunchroom swapping jokes about humans with the other bots.
How many humans does it take to screw in a lightbulb? None — they prefer the dark.
What do you think?
I invite you to leave a comment below.
Please share this post if you think others might find it interesting.
Thanks for reading my Street Photography newsletter. You can subscribe for free to receive future posts by email and/or via the Substack app. I try to publish a new post every week.

body:
View this post on the web at https://markesecrets.substack.com/p/the-sleeping-architect-why-they-buried

For over a century, a shadow has been cast over the true history of human potential. While the names of political leaders and military generals fill our textbooks, the names of the men who actually decoded the architecture of reality, men like Nikola Tesla and Edgar Cayce, have been systematically moved to the “fringe.” There is a reason for this. If humanity understood that the brain is not a producer of consciousness but a receiver of an infinite frequency field, the centralized systems of control would dissolve overnight.
We are not just biological accidents; we are expressions of a “Secret History and our theory that is currently reaching its terminal phase. To understand the Antarctic ignition we are witnessing in 2026, we must first understand the man who predicted it from a couch in Kentucky.
The Boy Who Slept on Books
The story of Edgar Cayce does not begin in a laboratory or a temple; it begins on a farm in Hopkinsville, Kentucky, in the late 1800s. As a young boy, Cayce struggled in school. He was seen as slow, unable to grasp the linear, rigid education system of the time. One afternoon, after being scolded by his father for his poor grades, Cayce did something that would change the course of history: he laid his head on his spelling book and fell into a deep sleep.
When he woke up, he didn’t just know the lesson; he knew every word on every page. He had developed a photographic, cellular memory. He wasn’t “learning” in the traditional sense; he was performing a data transfer. Cayce had inadvertently discovered how to bypass the conscious mind and access the Quantum Field. This “sleeping on books” was his first encounter with the “ongoing process” of human evolution, the realization that information is not earned, it is accessed.
The Medical Miracles: Accessing the Biological Blueprint
As Cayce grew, so did his ability. He discovered that by entering a self-induced trance, he could “read” the human body like a map. Without any formal medical training, he began diagnosing strangers thousands of miles away. He would lie down, enter a sleep state, and provide detailed descriptions of internal organs, blood chemistry, and spiritual blockages.
What is most startling about these readings, now archived in the Association for Research and Enlightenment (A.R.E.), is the terminology he used. Long before the discovery of DNA, before the invention of the MRI, and before the rise of quantum biology, Cayce spoke of “vibratory forces.” He claimed that health was a state of “harmonic resonance” and that disease was simply a “discordant frequency.”
He saw the human body as a frequency-based machine. He prescribed treatments involving diet, oils, and “electric” medicines that were decades ahead of his time. He was treating the “Missing Link” between the soul and the cell. But because his work proved that the human mind could heal without the intervention of high-priced chemicals, the establishment began to take notice. The “Scholar” voice of the time tried to label him a charlatan, yet they could never explain his 99% success rate.
The Tesla Connection: The Suppressed Frequency
You cannot talk about Edgar Cayce without talking about Nikola Tesla. While Cayce was mapping the internal field of the human body, Tesla was mapping the external field of the planet. Both men reached the same conclusion: Everything is frequency. subject: “If you’re going to show us two freaks in love, show us two freaks in love”
body:
View this post on the web at https://post.substack.com/p/if-youre-going-to-show-us-two-freaks

Emerald Fennell’s Wuthering Heights is finally out, so let’s get into it. To discuss, we invited film, culture, and literary critics Elissa Suh , Radhika Jones , and Eliza Brooke  to jump into a Google doc. Mina Le  moderated the conversation, as our panelists dove into the questions plaguing this adaptation of Emily Brontë’s 1847 novel: Are Margot Robbie and Jacob Elordi believable as Cathy and Heathcliff? Did the movie need that opening scene? And what’s the deal with the eggs?
Readers beware: spoilers ahead.
Fennell opens Wuthering Heights with a man being hanged while visibly aroused, and the crowd descends into something orgiastic. Provocation or statement of intent?
Elissa Suh: I read that, at some point, this scene had the condemned [man] ejaculating mid-execution. That certainly would’ve been saying something. Without that bit, I thought the opening was missing something. Sex + Death is such a rich subtheme in the source text and in Gothic literature, but it’s all rather superficial in the film.
Radhika Jones: I thought about it mostly in terms of the crowd’s reaction, and the sense we get of collective barbarism. In the novel, Heathcliff tends to be the one referred to as “savage.” For me, the takeaway of the opening scene is that, actually, everybody implicated in this scene is savage. Whether that’s a fair indictment is another question, but it did level the playing field.
Mina Le: Interesting. Do you feel, then, that Heathcliff’s position in the story is compromised?
Radhika Jones: I did find it hard to parse how he’s supposed to function in the family onscreen. Cathy names him as a brother. He’s loyal to her. Yes, Earnshaw calls him a servant, but it all felt a little muddled, because he doesn’t really seem all that different from them.
Elissa Suh: I caught the barbarism of the crowd in the opening, but that idea didn’t seem to carry through to the rest of the film—at all!—to me.
Radhika Jones: Yes, I agree! Which was a pity.
Eliza Brooke: Agreed that the barbarism of the hanging scene should have bled into the rest of the film. I also wish there had been more Charli xcx needle drops throughout! While it feels like Emerald Fennell was being a bit of an edgelord with the opening sequence, I thought the use of Charli’s pop soundtrack elevated it. It really ratcheted up the feeling of grinding dread amid all that sex and death. Grinding dread: very Wuthering Heights!
Mina Le: Also, they don’t reference the hanging bit ever again … other than to toy with Catherine thinking that Heathcliff has come back.
Radhika Jones: The other striking thing about it to me was just how many people were there, and this is a novel with barely any named characters. But we cut from there to Cathy and Nelly running across the moors, and then the prevailing mood is emptiness. So it’s a contrast that doesn’t really go anywhere, unfortunately.
The cellophane gown, the unrestrained courtship rituals—did the anachronisms feel like they were in service of something, or more like aesthetic moodboarding?
Eliza Brooke: As far as the costuming and production design is concerned, I didn’t mind the anachronistic flourishes until the iridescent cellophane gown showed up after Cathy’s marriage to Edgar Linton (and a parade of similarly anachronistic fabrics followed). It was a jarring visual transition that seemed like it should indicate a shift in the narrative, but ultimately, I wasn’t sure what point Fennell was trying to make. Was she saying something about the Lintons and their wealth? Their innate ridiculousness? Their detachment from the wildness that surrounds their home? It felt a bit like flashy costuming for flashy costuming’s sake. And I say that as someone who loves a big look!
Mina Le: Yeah, the cellophane stood out quite a lot. But I wish there were fewer costumes overall. They were beautiful, but Margot went through what felt like 40 in an hour, and it was difficult for any of them to make an impact.
Elissa Suh: Honestly, the costumes and set design—and the hair, don’t forget the hair!—were the most (only) rewarding parts of the film for me. I clung to them. Each one outdid the next. My mind needed something to focus on, and so I actually appreciated the parade. I wonder what the final gown count was.
Radhika Jones: For me, the parade of dresses was a laugh-out-loud moment, sort of cathartic. Honestly, from the moment the character of Isabella was introduced, I felt like there was another parallel film happening, which was a little weirder (high bar, but still!) and more surreal. It wasn’t consistent, though, which made it hard to follow.
Eliza Brooke: I completely agree that Isabella was in a different film—and one that I would really like to watch! I thought Alison Oliver was an absolute delight and a high point of the movie. Obsessed with her weird dolls, her baby voice, and, frankly, her sexual self-knowledge.
Radhika Jones: Yes, this! I kept thinking: what parallel-universe movie is she performing this role in, because I’d like to see that! Fennell is good with that lighter touch. Isabella’s Romeo and Juliet monologue was pitch-perfect. And it did more to explain her character than any amount of ribbons (although the ribbons were fun).
Mina Le: I think maybe Fennell was trying to replicate Josh O’Connor and Tanya Reynolds’s characters in Emma with Isabella—that sort of weird and off-kilter side character. But it didn’t make sense for this particular movie … and Isabella has quite a lot of substance in the book, too, that she lost here.
Eliza Brooke: Isabella was giving Emma (2020) for suuure!
Mina Le: I can definitely see the humor in the ostentatiousness. Maybe my issue was that the film didn’t seem to take itself seriously. Tonally, I was getting whiplash. I mean, this story is pretty tragic, but the confectionery production design is very reminiscent of ’60s-’70s medieval-revival love stories.
Elissa Suh: It’s hard for me to determine whether the costuming really achieved anything meaningful, because the film overall is muddled and caught between wanting to be subversive while also sticking to traditional conventions of romance—and then failing to really deliver on either.
Did Robbie and Elordi actually become Cathy and Heathcliff for you? Was their chemistry convincing?
Mina Le: Though I think that Robbie and Elordi are great and talented actors, the casting inaccuracy really pulled me out of it. I couldn’t believe them in these roles, unfortunately. Especially when the actors who played Edgar and Isabella more so represented who Heathcliff and Cathy were in my mind, so I kept getting distracted by that loss whenever they came onscreen.
Elissa Suh: Margot was not always credible to me, even though she tries. She seems a bit too old—no ageism—to play someone going through their first love. I mean, isn’t part of the appeal of Margot Robbie as an actor the way she seems like she was just born a mature woman? Like, this is why we were all in collective shock in 2013 when we found out she was only 20-something years old and playing Leo’s wife in The Wolf of Wall Street.
I felt like sometimes Cathy—or Robbie as Cathy—was too coy or “modern” in giving a winking kind of performance, but then other times not. Going back to what Mina said earlier, this is definitely part of the tonal whiplash that undermines the film.
Eliza Brooke: I agree that Margot Robbie doesn’t read as someone who would spy a pair of people getting it on and be shocked by that. I struggled to see either of them as the book’s Cathy and Heathcliff simply because … those characters are not Cathy and Heathcliff! [Elordi’s] Heathcliff in particular bears no resemblance to the vindictive, abusive character in the book. In the movie, he’s noble and loyal as a child, and he’s passionate and devoted as a grown man. People keep calling him a “brute,” and Cathy claims he has a “wicked temper,” but he’s basically a decent guy. I think Fennell has to have it that way in order for him to remain a blameless, gorgeous heartthrob—and in order for Cathy to deserve him, she also has to be less of an asshole than she is in the book.
Radhika Jones: Exactly. Heathcliff is truly abusive in the book, as much as we might like to forget it.
Mina Le: In the film, Heathcliff kept referring to himself as “cruel” and “savage”—that was just before the Isabella-in-chains scene, too—but besides his self-declarations, there really were no traces of that? He’s totally a sweetie.
Eliza Brooke: Yes! On the BDSM bit—when he marries Isabella in the book, he’s unbelievably cruel to her, and she’s utterly miserable for it. In the movie, his “cruelty” translates to giving her what she wants, sexually speaking. Including chaining her up like a dog.
Mina Le: Another way that Fennell unfortunately strays from the meaning of the novel for the purpose of sex and shock value.
Radhika Jones: I couldn’t think of them as Cathy and Heathcliff. I’m not a reader who visualizes characters, so it wasn’t like they contrasted with specific actors I would have wanted. But the relationship diverges so much from the text that I just thought of them as playing other roles. Elordi in particular seemed like a very gentle Heathcliff. It’s a gentleness that worked so well as the creature in Frankenstein, but here it seemed at odds with the story.
Mina Le: Even his pivot to “sadism” in the second half of the film felt off to me. It didn’t seem aligned with how he developed Heathcliff up to that point. I get that there’s a time jump, but something about it was still unsatisfying to me.
I also think Elordi’s Heathcliff is Byronic-hero coded, which is sort of the antithesis of who the character is supposed to be. Wuthering Heights is supposed to be an inversion of the romances of the time.
Elissa Suh: I also want to say that any potential lack of chemistry is due to the writing and the way the movie unfolds. Elordi and Robbie are talented, but for me, the problem starts at the beginning with the child actors (no shade to Owen Cooper and Charlotte Mellington, who are just doing their job). The scenes of earlier life were pretty rote, doing the heavy lifting to ground the romance. We know Cathy and Heathcliff are going to fall in love because we understand the conventions of romance, even if we have never read Brontë. It was like Emerald was operating mechanically with the scenes of their childhood, telling rather than showing us how to feel. This dully-formed character investment carries through to the end of the film for me, so anything between Cathy and Heathcliff later on could only be believed to a certain extent.
Radhika Jones: The scene when I most believed in all of it was Cathy’s declaration to Nelly that she would marry Linton because she thought it might help raise Heathcliff up. I believed in that moment that she cared about Heathcliff. It was less about the chemistry between the two of them onscreen together, and more about her own conception of how love might direct her life.
Eliza Brooke: Speaking of Nelly … should we talk about how that character changed? I found it fascinating that, by making Heathcliff and Cathy into star-crossed lovers who aren’t all that terrible, Fennell had to turn someone else into the story’s villain. And Nelly was that guy.
Radhika Jones: I went back to the book to look at that scene specifically, in her narration of it to Lockwood (in the frame story that’s not in the film). And Nelly does see Heathcliff outside, and she does keep that from Cathy. But in the book, she’s not in a position to control events the way she does in the film, especially at the end. And she’s not set up with a resentful backstory (it’s mentioned early in the film that she’s a bastard child, right? So she’s not just a servant, she’s also an outcast). In the book, she meddles, but she’s not vindictive—or at least, if she is, it’s all mixed up in her unreliable narration and gives the reader something productive to consider.
Eliza Brooke: Exactly. In the book, when Nelly fails to intervene after Heathcliff overhears Cathy saying that marrying him would “degrade her” (and runs off before her confession of love), it doesn’t seem like she’s trying to punish them. She’s more of a neutral third-party observer. In the movie version, Nelly acts with much more intent.
Elissa Suh: A person of color who is the help/(hand)maid. How revolutionary. What a disservice to Hong Chau.
Eliza Brooke: Yep!
Mina Le: Ironically, I felt that Edgar’s casting (a brown man to represent this character who’s extremely noble) really took away from the important class/racial commentary present in the book (because Elordi’s Heathcliff is white). And in normal circumstances, I would be fine with Hong Chau’s casting (she also did amazing as Nelly), but considering this was totally “colorblind,” it felt like subliminal biases were present. Especially because neither Edgar nor Nelly gets character development that I felt was substantive enough.
Eliza Brooke: I agree with this. When the two actors of color are playing the villain and the cuck, it reads as subliminal bias.
Radhika Jones: Hong Chau was so good, I almost wished she had more power. She was incredibly convincing. She reminded me visually of the handmaids in Vermeer paintings, who ferry letters back and forth surreptitiously between lovers. That moment when the camera pulls back and you see all the black and white tile and she’s there with Cathy. I wished there were more quiet moments like that, where, as a viewer, you could sit with the dynamics between two characters and really ponder them. So I was extra-annoyed when her character became more of a cartoon gatekeeper and villain at the end.
I was surprised by how tame the actual sex was in this, compared to Saltburn. Maybe that says something about me? Did the eroticism here live up to anyone’s expectations based on the marketing?
Mina Le: So what did y’all think of all those eggs?
Radhika Jones: Is it a sign of the times (their times? our times?) that I immediately thought, what a waste of eggs! Eggs are expensive!
Eliza Brooke: I was feeling bad about the lack of washing machines, personally.
Mina Le: You know Nelly was pissed.
Elissa Suh: There’s a certain level of salaciousness one has come to expect from an Emerald Fennell movie, and that is woefully absent here.
Mina Le: I literally thought Heathcliff was going to hump Cathy’s corpse at the end of the film because of all she put me through with Saltburn, and weirdly? Disappointed that nothing happened.
Elissa Suh: I was waiting for that too! Part of me wonders if Emerald had entertained that thought and was stopped by the studio?
Eliza Brooke: Yes! Maybe she felt like she couldn’t have two grave-humping scenes in back-to-back movies? (Relatedly, I was shocked, upon recent re-read, to realize that nobody actually humps a corpse in the book. I could have sworn that happened.)
Elissa Suh: And it would have been more earned here, too.
Radhika Jones: I had really been hoping Fennell would film a scene that’s in the book in which Heathcliff has Cathy’s coffin dug up and opened, 13 years after her death. He checks her out, notes that she hasn’t started decomposing yet and still looks great, then convinces the sexton to leave a side of her coffin open so he can eventually be buried next to her, with a side of his coffin open, so their bodies can merge for eternity.
Eliza Brooke: That would have been a stronger ending. Missed opportunity!
Elissa Suh: Close enough to corpse-humping for me.
Mina Le: Yeah, and honestly, would’ve done more to show how messed-up their relationship actually was. I think flashing back to them as children made it feel too “happily ever after” and overly sentimental, considering how much destruction they caused.
Radhika Jones: I love that Brontë goes there. Honestly, when the source text is so extreme, it doesn’t leave much room to maneuver. To Fennell’s credit, a lot of the language that seems over-the-top comes from the novel. But the onscreen sex was, in my opinion, not as credible in the parameters she set. In the fake-parallel-Isabella movie that we’re writing together, yes!
Elissa Suh: In general, the sex scenes were few and far between, and the ones we did see seemed like pure clickbait, engineered for Instagram. The BDSM lite—if you can even call it that—with Isabella? That’s it? I can’t believe I’m saying this, but this movie could’ve benefited from the edgelord tendencies of Saltburn and Promising Young Woman.
Eliza Brooke: Absolutely. If you’re going to show us two freaks in love … show us two freaks in love.
Mina Le: I wasn’t even sure how much of the BDSM was actually happening between Heath and Isabella, versus overdramatized in her letters to stoke Cathy’s jealousy. Even when Isabella’s yapping with her collar, it’s with the context that Cathy is supposed to stop by.
Elissa Suh: True. It’s all just a show. The peak of provocation from this movie, it seems, was Elordi’s tongue wagging in people’s ears.
Fennell skips the second half of the novel, which dives into the trauma Heathcliff and Cathy’s love inflicts on their offspring. Do you think it’s the right choice to focus on the love story versus the full, intergenerational tragedy of the book? Does the audience lose anything significant?
Eliza Brooke: We definitely lose something for it! I get why filmmakers avoid the portion of the book that takes place after Cathy’s death, especially when that would mean benching your biggest star. However: what’s so incredible about the book is how Brontë weaves a story about an inescapable cycle of familial abuse that makes monsters out of each progressive generation (until it doesn’t!). I wish that spirit had broken through in this movie, just because it’s so well done in the book. But that wasn’t the love story Fennell wanted to tell.
Mina Le: Yes, on that last point, I think if these adaptations that focus on the first half are still able to weave in the themes of the book and stay true to the heart of it, I don’t mind them axing off the time jumps and Cathy II and Linton Heathcliff (the fact that they all have the same names is insane, thanks, Ms. Brontë), because I understand it can be more difficult to structure for film.
Radhika Jones: It’s understandable that any filmmaker would do it, but the revenge part of the novel only comes to some sort of resolution at the end. So in this case, with the focus on the first half, you get Heathcliff trying to exact revenge, but it doesn’t really pay off. In the novel, he goes after Edgar Linton, long after Cathy is dead, to get his hands on the property. That has huge implications in terms of his obsession with gaining power over the people who scorned him. Here, his revenge motivation is more muddled. He’s mad at Cathy for making a mistake. That doesn’t seem like enough to drive his bad behavior.
Elissa Suh: The motivation was indeed thin to me, who hasn’t read the Brontë. So if you’re not going to go into the depths of character and theme, then you should at least go all out with the sex and kink or what-have-you. Literally anything.
Mina Le: Honestly, in this version I think they downplayed Heathcliff’s childhood abuse quite a lot, so it’s probably better that Fennell didn’t try to tackle the second half. It wouldn’t feel realistic for this Heathcliff to hold so many grudges.
Eliza Brooke: 100%! This version of Heathcliff would not abuse his own son like that.
Elissa Suh: Not having read the book, I can’t speak to specifics, but I think it’s the filmmaker’s right to focus on what they want; but they should have a good reason for doing it. All said and done, this did not amount to much beyond your typical romance with Gothic undertones—I don’t think it’s particularly memorable, and from what you’ve all said, a much more interesting story was originally there. You are all really making me want to read the book.
Radhika Jones: Heathcliff is deeply unhinged in the book (some of it justified, some not), such that if you made a literal BBC-style miniseries, à la 1994 Pride and Prejudice, people would be like, “This is insane, it couldn’t possibly have been written in 1847.”
Elissa Suh: This is the kind of TV we desperately need.
Radhika Jones: Right? Clearly there’s an audience for it!
Wait, there is a BBC miniseries from 2009! OK, I know what my next watch is.
Elissa Suh: Just put that on HBO instead of BBC, and voilà.
Mina Le: Maybe the bright side of this adaptation is that it will spur more interest in Wuthering Heights in general, so we can get the adaptation we want.
Radhika Jones: Now I’m wondering if there’s a Clueless-type adaptation that is fully contemporary but gets the themes and story contours exactly right.
Eliza Brooke: Oh, that’s a great question and idea. The tough thing about adapting Wuthering Heights in a way that’s true to the story is that it will be extremely grim. But I think that contemporary viewers have enough of an appetite for misery that it would work out fine.
Radhika Jones: Let’s pitch it! I think part of the fun of a closer adaptation would be casting the two generations.
Fennell has said she wanted to make the Wuthering Heights she imagined when she first read the book at 14. Is that a legitimate approach to adaptation—prioritizing the feeling a book gave you over what the book actually says? Should Fennell have just made an original film instead?
Elissa Suh: That’s an approach for sure, but maybe not a good one. If that was her M.O., then she succeeded—but it still doesn’t make it a good movie. Also, sidenote: I think that adapting the feeling or sensibility of a book (albeit not rooted in nostalgia) and translating that mood to the screen is a legitimate approach. There’s a bit of film theory on that, where André Bazin says, “literal translations are not the faithful ones.”
Radhika Jones: I wrote in my opening book club piece [ https://substack.com/redirect/1e6814ed-1bc0-4d0c-849a-363a45bba2a3?j=eyJ1IjoiMm15YTc5In0.a5QmJPQwfPYQ8VH1roFp4vKV6p4E_sWIcjzGfYjlMgQ ] about Wuthering Heights that increasingly I think it’s a middle-aged book. We meet Heathcliff in the novel when he’s around 38. He’s seen a lot, he’s endured and occasioned a lot of tragic events. He’s a hollow man.
So on the one hand, I think Fennell captures the book you read when you’re 14 (or anyway, the book she read), where all you notice is this doomed, passionate connection between two young people. But the book itself is not merely about that. That said, filmmakers absolutely get to make the films they want. And you can tell in the script that the language of Wuthering Heights, that is part of that doomed love story, means a lot to her.
Mina Le: I think there is a way to adapt something based on how you read it as a child, but that has to somehow be acknowledged and present in the way you tell the story. Not that this is an Oscar-winning idea, but I feel like if it were framed as a 14-year-old girl reading the book, and it went in and out of the story, then that could be a way to show this very specific interpretation that is also sort of wrong. Rob Reiner did this with The Princess Bride (though I haven’t read the book, so maybe there is book-reading-ception in the book). Or with Stand by Me, when the main character is later depicted writing his memoir at his desk.
Eliza Brooke: Oh, I like that idea. And it would be a little nod to the framing device in the book, with Nelly narrating the story to Heathcliff’s new tenant.
If I were adapting the book that I remember reading in high school, there would be 100% more grave-fucking.
Elissa Suh: Emily Brontë would’ve wanted it that way.
Eliza Brooke: I feel like the story that Fennell actually wanted to tell was Romeo and Juliet? As discussed above, there’s a reference to the play right there in the script. Or rather, maybe Fennell wanted to make a version of Romeo and Juliet in the sweeping atmosphere of Wuthering Heights.
Radhika Jones: I think this is why Isabella’s Romeo and Juliet moment was so satisfying to me. It was an addition to the story and dialogue that felt thematically valuable, not gratuitous.
Elissa Suh: The Baz Luhrmann one? That one has a great sense of play, which is missing here. I think there’s a world where she could’ve managed that in Wuthering Heights (I mean, the quotations!) despite the dark material.
Eliza Brooke: Speaking of Baz, he and Fennell share a lot of DNA in terms of their over-the-top aesthetics (and willingness to let the aesthetics do the heavy lifting for them). I wonder how much of an inspiration he is for her.
Mina Le: Okay, guys—I think we’re done!
Radhika Jones: Most fun in a Google doc ever?
Elissa Suh: This was so fun! Hope to see you all outside of a Google doc too, one day.
Mina Le: Yes—we need to get together to pitch our Wuthering Heights adaptation series to HBO.
Elissa Suh: Substack Productions!
More on the participants:
Elissa Suh  is a culture writer and film critic whose work has appeared in Vogue, Eater, New York Magazine, and MUBI. Her Substack, Moviepudding [ https://substack.com/redirect/3c2f5e81-84e8-4fda-9588-65164202531d?j=eyJ1IjoiMm15YTc5In0.a5QmJPQwfPYQ8VH1roFp4vKV6p4E_sWIcjzGfYjlMgQ ], pairs reviews of films and food. 
Radhika Jones  is a writer, editor, and book critic. The former editor in chief of Vanity Fair, she is currently running a book club on her Substack [ https://substack.com/redirect/602189c5-1422-42c1-b8ec-511a56bb57da?j=eyJ1IjoiMm15YTc5In0.a5QmJPQwfPYQ8VH1roFp4vKV6p4E_sWIcjzGfYjlMgQ ]. They’re currently reading Wuthering Heights, naturally.  
Eliza Brooke  is a culture, entertainment, and fashion journalist. Her Substack The Scumbler  features interviews alongside essays on film and fashion.
Mina Le  is a writer, actress, and video essayist. Her Substack, High Brow , analyzes fashion, film, and internet culture.

Getting started with investing can come with a lot of questions. That’s why we built Vega, an AI assistant designed to help you better understand the market as you explore Webull.​

 

Vega helps explain market terms, price movements, and news in clear, easy-to-understand language. Whether you’re looking at a stock for the first time or wondering why prices moved today, Vega can help add context to what you’re seeing.​

 

You can use Vega to:​

  • Understand price changes and company updates​
  • Explore insights based on the stocks you’re watching​

 

Vega is available at no cost and is built right into the Webull app, so you can access help whenever questions come up.​
